---
title: "Quiz: regularisation and data augmentation"
---

Short questions on overfitting, regularisation and augmentation. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

---

**Q1.** A network reaches 100 % on its 20 training images and 68 % on validation images. Weight decay raises the validation loss less, but the accuracy stays at 68 %. Why can weight decay not fix this?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What is missing from the 20 training images?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Weight decay makes memorising harder, but it cannot add information. If the training images lack some variation (here: cells in other directions), the network cannot learn that this variation does not matter. Augmentation (or more data) supplies it.
:::

---

**Q2.** Name the augmentation that tells the network each of the following does not matter: (a) the direction of a cell; (b) the brightness of the microscope; (c) the exact shape of the cell outline; (d) focus.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Geometric or intensity?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
(a) Rotations and flips. (b) Gain and offset (and gamma). (c) Elastic deformation. (d) A small random blur.
:::

---

**Q3.** For a segmentation network, which augmentations must also be applied to the mask, and which must not?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Do the pixels move, or only their values?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Geometric ones (flips, rotations, zoom, elastic) must be applied to the mask with exactly the same transformation (nearest-neighbour sampling for labels). Intensity changes, noise and blur change only the image; the mask stays.
:::

---

**Q4.** You measure GFP expression from the mean intensity of each cell. Is random gain (±30 %) a good augmentation for the cell **segmentation** network? For a network that **predicts the expression level**?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Augment with what varies, never with what you measure.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
For segmentation, yes: the outline does not depend on the brightness. For predicting the expression level, no: intensity is the readout, and the augmentation would teach the network to ignore it.
:::

---

**Q5.** Why is it a leak to augment the whole data set first and split it into training and test sets afterwards?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Where do the copies of a test image end up?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Rotated and flipped copies of the test images land in the training set: the network has seen them, and the test accuracy is too optimistic. Split first, then augment only the training images, on the fly.
:::

---

**Q6.** The microscope has a fixed, known pixel size. Why can a zoom augmentation by ×0.5 to ×2 hurt?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What does the apparent size of an object tell the network?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
At a fixed pixel size, size is information: a nucleus of 50 pixels is a nucleus, one of 100 pixels may be something else. Zooming by 2 creates objects of sizes that never occur and makes size useless as a cue. Zoom only within the real variation.
:::

---

**Q7.** *(math)* Weight decay $\lambda = 0.001$ with plain gradient descent and $\eta = 0.1$. By which factor is every weight shrunk per step? After 10,000 steps without any data gradient?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
The gradient of $\lambda w^2$ is $2\lambda w$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$1 - 2\eta\lambda = 0.9998$ per step; $0.9998^{10000} = e^{-2} \approx 0.14$.
:::
